nameStory: The red-eye round herring gets its name from two distinctive features that make it stand out from other herring-like fish. Its eyes have a characteristic reddish tint that becomes quite noticeable when you see the fish up close, while its belly has the rounded shape typical of its family rather than the sharp, knife-like edge of true herrings.
description: The red-eye round herring is a small, silvery fish that belongs to a family known for their distinctively rounded bellies. Unlike the sharp-keeled bellies of true herrings, this fish has a smooth, curved underside that feels rounded when you handle it. These fish typically grow to about 6-8 inches in length and have the streamlined, torpedo-like shape common to many oceanic schooling fish. They're quite rare in New England waters, making any sighting particularly noteworthy.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctively rounded belly that feels smooth and curved when touched, lacking the sharp ridge or 'keel' found on true herrings

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silvery sides with a darker blue-green back, and notably reddish-tinted eyes that catch the light

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish typically 6-8 inches long, fitting comfortably in your palm with a slender, streamlined build

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single dorsal fin positioned roughly in the middle of the back, with clear to slightly yellowish fins that feel delicate to touch

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in open ocean waters rather than close to shore, usually swimming in schools in the water column

habitat: Red-eye round herrings are oceanic fish that prefer the open waters off New England's coast rather than nearshore areas. They're typically found in deeper, cooler waters where they school in the mid-water column, feeding on small planktonic organisms. When encountered in New England, it's usually far offshore in the Gulf of Maine or beyond the continental shelf.

seasonality.spring: May appear in offshore waters as ocean temperatures begin to warm, though sightings remain extremely rare in New England waters.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season for potential sightings in warmer offshore waters, particularly during upwelling events that bring nutrient-rich water to the surface.
seasonality.fall: May follow food sources closer to the continental shelf as water temperatures begin to cool and plankton distributions shift.
seasonality.winter: Typically moves to deeper, warmer waters well offshore and away from New England's coastal areas.

funFact: Despite being called a 'herring,' this fish is so distantly related to true herrings that scientists place it in a completely different family - it's more like a herring-shaped impostor that evolved similar looks for life in the open ocean!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young true herrings or sardines, but the rounded belly is the dead giveaway - run your finger along the underside and if it feels smooth and curved rather than sharp-edged like a knife, you've found something special. Remember: 'Round herring, round belly.'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'herring' in this case is misleading - this fish belongs to the rainbow sardine family (Dussumieriidae), not the true herring family (Clupeidae). This is a classic case of common names being based on superficial similarity rather than actual family relationships, much like how killer whales aren't actually whales but dolphins.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus found in New England waters, compare it to its closest family relatives, the rainbow sardines. Red-eye round herrings are distinguished by their more elongated body shape and the characteristic reddish eye coloration. Within the broader herring-like fishes, the rounded belly immediately sets it apart from all true herrings, sardines, and anchovies found in regional waters.
